problem: The Schema & Structured Data for WP & AMP plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to PHP Object Injection in versions up to, and including, 1.68. This is due to deserialization of untrusted input via the admin export (saswp_export_all_settings_and_schema) which calls unrestricted unserialize() on every raw post meta value, combined with saswp_review_form_process_data() which stores unauthenticated-visitor-supplied reviewer-name data through update_post_meta — the plugin sanitizes with sanitize_text_field(), which does not recognise PHP serialization syntax or the NUL property-name delimiters, and WordPress's maybe_serialize/is_serialized has no case for the legacy PHP 'C' custom-serialization token (ArrayObject), so the payload is persisted byte-for-byte and never wrapped in a protective extra serialize layer. solution: Never deserialize untrusted data; require signed/integrity-checked payloads. Update to the patched version.

This makes it possible for authenticated attackers with Author-level access or above to permanently delete any WordPress attachment in the media library, including media files owned by other users along with their associated files on disk, regardless of ownership — a capability not available through the normal WordPress interface. The revert nonce is exposed via `wp_localize_script` on `/wp-admin/upload.php` to any user with `upload_files` capability, ensuring the nonce check that is present does not serve as a meaningful barrier to Author-level exploitation. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Canonicalize paths and restrict to an allowlisted directory. Update to the patched version.

The payload must be encoded as C-style escape sequences (e.g. \x3c/\x3e) at storage time so that wp_kses_post — applied on save for users lacking unfiltered_html — passes it through without stripping angle brackets; WordPress core's shortcode_parse_atts() then decodes the escapes into real HTML characters at render time. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Encode all user-controlled output, enforce a strict Content-Security-Policy, and update to the patched version.

problem: Flowintel contains a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in its HedgeDoc case-notes integration. When a user with editor or administrator privileges associates a HedgeDoc URL with a case, the application later issues a server-side HTTP GET request to that URL to retrieve note content. Before the fix, the stored URL was used directly without validation of its scheme, host, port, path, or userinfo, and the HTTP client followed redirects by default with no connect or read timeouts. An authenticated attacker could therefore cause the Flowintel server to issue requests to arbitrary internal or external endpoints (for example, cloud instance-metadata services, internal management interfaces, or other intranet hosts) and receive the response body, or follow a redirect chain to an unintended destination. The absence of timeouts also permitted resource-exhaustion against the server's outbound connection pool. Preconditions: - An authenticated account with editor or administrator role on the target case. - The HedgeDoc integration feature is enabled (no explicit configuration gate existed before the fix). Impact: - Disclosure of sensitive data served by internal or cloud-metadata endpoints. - Potential denial of service through unbounded outbound requests. Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Allowlist and validate all input server-side before use. Update to the patched version.

problem: The system call verifier z_vrfy_k_thread_stack_space_get() in kernel/thread.c checked the result of K_SYSCALL_OBJ(thread, K_OBJ_THREAD) with the CHECKIF() macro instead of K_OOPS(). CHECKIF() compiles to if (0) when CONFIG_NO_RUNTIME_CHECKS is selected, and becomes an assertion when CONFIG_ASSERT_ON_ERRORS is selected. In both cases, the kernel-object validation result for the user-supplied thread pointer is ignored, or is a no-op when assertions are disabled. On builds with CONFIG_USERSPACE, CONFIG_INIT_STACKS and CONFIG_THREAD_STACK_INFO plus one of those check modes, a user-mode thread can call k_thread_stack_space_get() with an arbitrary pointer. That pointer can be a fake struct k_thread in its own memory, or a thread object it has no permission on. z_impl_k_thread_stack_space_get() then dereferences thread->stack_info in supervisor mode and scans memory starting at the attacker-chosen stack_info.start. The syscall returns the number of leading 0xAA bytes at that address. This gives an unprivileged thread a limited oracle on arbitrary kernel or peripheral memory, and allows privileged reads of attacker-selected addresses, including MMIO. No write primitive results. The default CONFIG_RUNTIME_ERROR_CHECKS configuration is not affected. The fix replaces the CHECKIF() with K_OOPS() so the object check is always enforced. Requires local access to exploit.
